title: Sliding Window Maximum — monotonic deque maintaining decreasing order.
shortTitle: Sliding Window Maximum — Monotonic Deque Maintaining Decreasing Order

s1_definition.profdef: Sliding Window Maximum returns the maximum of every contiguous window of size K as the window slides across an array. A monotonic deque of indices, kept in decreasing order of their values, gives the current window maximum at the front in O(1); each index is pushed and popped at most once, so the whole computation is O(n) time and O(K) space.
s1_definition.analogy: The National Bank of India tracks a rolling K-minute peak of transaction rates. Rajesh keeps a short queue of candidate peak times, always ordered so the biggest is at the front. When a new, larger rate arrives it knocks out every smaller candidate behind it, and when a candidate falls out of the time window it is removed from the front.
s1_definition.oneliner: Keep a deque of indices with decreasing values; the front is always the window maximum, and each index enters and leaves at most once.
s1_definition.raw:
**Professional definition:** Sliding Window Maximum returns the maximum of every contiguous window of size K as the window slides across an array. A monotonic deque of indices, kept in decreasing order of their values, gives the current window maximum at the front in O(1); each index is pushed and popped at most once, so the whole computation is O(n) time and O(K) space.

**In simple words (banking analogy):** The National Bank of India tracks a rolling K-minute peak of transaction rates. Rajesh keeps a short queue of candidate peak times, always ordered so the biggest is at the front. When a new, larger rate arrives it knocks out every smaller candidate behind it, and when a candidate falls out of the time window it is removed from the front.

**One line to remember:** Keep a deque of indices with decreasing values; the front is always the window maximum, and each index enters and leaves at most once.

sections.s2_technical:
Use an `ArrayDeque<Integer>` holding array indices, maintained so the values at those indices are strictly decreasing from front to back. For each new index `r`: first, pop from the back while the value at the back index is less than or equal to `a[r]`, because those can never be the maximum while `a[r]` is in the window. Then push `r` to the back. Next, remove the front index if it has slid out of the window, meaning `front <= r - k`. Finally, once `r >= k - 1`, the value at the front index is the maximum of the current window.

A code snippet on transaction rates: `int[] maxWindow(int[] a, int k) { Deque<Integer> dq = new ArrayDeque<>(); int[] out = new int[a.length - k + 1]; for (int r=0; r<a.length; r++) { while (!dq.isEmpty() && a[dq.peekLast()] <= a[r]) dq.pollLast(); dq.offerLast(r); if (dq.peekFirst() <= r - k) dq.pollFirst(); if (r >= k - 1) out[r - k + 1] = a[dq.peekFirst()]; } return out; }`.

Why store indices and not values? Because the eviction from the front depends on position, so you must know where each candidate sits to tell when it leaves the window. The decreasing-order invariant guarantees the front is the maximum: anything smaller that arrived earlier was already popped when a larger value came in, so only genuine candidates remain, newest-and-smaller toward the back.

The linear time is the key result. Although there is an inner while loop, each index is added to the deque exactly once and removed at most once, so the total number of deque operations across the whole scan is bounded by two times n. A senior nuance is using `<=` rather than `<` on the back-pop so equal values do not linger uselessly, and remembering the front-eviction check uses the index, which is why storing indices rather than values is mandatory.
sections.s3_banking:
Problem 1 — The National Bank of India operations dashboard shows the rolling peak transaction rate over every K-minute window to spot load spikes. This is exactly how sliding-window-maximum works — the maximum of each sliding window.

Problem 2 — The rate series streams continuously and is long, so recomputing each window's max naively would be too slow, and the monotonic deque gives each window's max in amortized constant time.

The code shows a `PeakRateAnalyzer` with `rollingMax`, a demo on a rate series with window size 3, and the array of window maxima.

sections.s5_journey:
Input: rates [1, 3, -1, -3, 5, 3, 6, 7], window size 3.

Step 1: Index 0 value 1, deque becomes [0]. Index 1 value 3, pop index 0 because 1 is at most 3, push 1, deque [1]. Index 2 value -1, not at most -1 so push, deque [1,2]; window full, front index 1 value 3 is the first max.

Step 2: Index 3 value -3, push, deque [1,2,3]; front index 1 is now at position r minus k which is 0, still inside, front value 3 is the max for window [3,-1,-3].

Step 3: Index 4 value 5, pop indices 3, 2, 1 since their values -3, -1, 3 are all at most 5, push 4, deque [4]; front value 5 is the max for window [-1,-3,5].

Step 4: Index 5 value 3, push, deque [4,5]; front 5 is the max for window [-3,5,3]. Index 6 value 6, pop 5 then 4 (values 3 and 5 at most 6), push 6, deque [6]; front 6 is max for window [5,3,6].

Step 5: Index 7 value 7, pop 6, push 7, deque [7]; front 7 is max for window [3,6,7]. The output array of window maxima is [3, 3, 5, 5, 6, 7].

```
2026-10-26 21:00:03 INFO    Rolling window maxima (k=3): [3, 3, 5, 5, 6, 7]
```
sections.s5b_flow:
```
  rates=[1,3,-1,-3,5,3,6,7] k=3
    │
    ▼
  deque of indices, values strictly decreasing front→back
    │ pop-back while a[back]<=a[r]; push r
    │ pop-front if front<=r-k
    │ front value = window max once r>=k-1
    ▼

```

sections.s6_takeaway:
Sliding Window Maximum returns the maximum of every window of size K as it slides across an array, and the efficient solution is a monotonic deque of indices kept in decreasing order of their values. For each new index I first pop from the back of the deque every index whose value is less than or equal to the new value, because those can never be the maximum while the larger new value is in the window, then I push the new index. I evict the front index if it has slid out of the window, and once the window is full the value at the front index is the maximum.

The reason I store indices rather than values is that evicting the front depends on position. I need to know where each candidate sits so I can tell exactly when it leaves the window, and that is impossible if I only kept values. The decreasing-order invariant is what makes the front always the maximum, because any smaller earlier value was already popped when a larger value arrived, so only real candidates remain with the newest and smallest toward the back.

The headline property is linear time. Even though there is an inner while loop, each index is pushed once and popped at most once, so the total deque work across the whole array is bounded by twice the length. I also use less-than-or-equal on the back pop rather than strict less-than so equal values do not linger uselessly.

In my banking project at the National Bank of India I used this in the operations dashboard to show the rolling peak transaction rate over every K-minute window and spot load spikes. Because the rate series streamed continuously and was long, recomputing each window's maximum naively would have been too slow, and the monotonic deque gave each window's maximum in amortized constant time. Explaining the decreasing-deque invariant, why indices are stored, and the amortized linear analysis shows the interviewer I understand the data-structure insight behind this hard problem.
